newsitem.title: JAPAN: BOBSLEIGH-SWISS DISQUALIFICATION UPHELD, GERMANY WINS FOUR-MAN.
newsitem.headline: BOBSLEIGH-SWISS DISQUALIFICATION UPHELD, GERMANY WINS FOUR-MAN.

text.p: A world championship bobsleigh race held more than three weeks ago in Switzerland was settled in a Japanese hotel on Tuesday when officials upheld disqualifications of the three Swiss top finishers.

Wolfgang Hoppes, fourth in St. Moritz, Switzerland, on February 2, was declared world champion by the International Bobsleigh Federation (FIBT). Hoppes had finished behind three Swiss competitors who were subsequently disqualified for equipment violations,
Fifth-place finisher Dirk Wiese was awarded the silver medal, while Brian Shimer of the United States, who placed sixth, won the bronze.
"I hope this is the first and last time that a world championship is decided at a table," said Wiese.
The disqualified Swiss entrants were Reto Goetschi, Christian Reich, and Marcel Rohner.

No further sanctions would be imposed on the Swiss team, said FIBT president Bob Storey, who urged federations to "do their best to remove any people from their organisations who believe the value of victory is more important than the value of sportsmanship."
Swiss Bobsleigh Federation president Giancarlo Torriani said the Swiss had submitted an appeal through the FIBT to the international sports tribunal in Lausanne, Switzerland.
"It's a slur we have to get struck from the record," Torriani said.
The FIBT had agreed in St. Moritz to delay confirmation of the race jury's unanimous ruling against the Swiss because of the uproar created by the decision.

The jury said the front axles of the Swiss sleds were illegal under international rules. The FIBT materials commission found in a routine post-race inspection that the three-piece front axles of the Swiss sleds were joined by screws.
Rohner's rear axle was also screwed.
Rules aimed at preventing the use of costly independent suspensions state that the axle must be a "continuous steel tube," which "may" be welded.
Materials commission member Bob Cuneo said the Swiss had used tape and putty to hide the joints.

The Swiss, who used the same sleds throughout the World Cup season, argued that rules did not specifically prohibit screws. Tape and putty was used on only one sled to waterproof the joint, said Torriani.

"The jury took one possible explanation of some words or phrases, but they didn't analyse all possibilities," said Swiss coach Janis Kipurs. "We need additional phrases in the rules to very specifically explain what is allowed or not allowed.
Kipurs said when Soviet teams were experimenting with new sleds in the early 1980s, juries would subsequently prohibit whatever changes increased speed.
Another Swiss coach Daniel Maag said the screwed axles did not increase sled speed. "It's only so it costs less when we have to replace it. We can change one piece instead of the whole thing."
U.S. head coach Steve Maiorca said allowing axle changes would result in a costly technology surge, putting smaller countries at a disadvantage.
"You've got to draw the line somewhere," said Maiorca.
